title: The Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP)
summary: Specifies the Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP), a web transfer protocol for very small devices and lossy, low-power networks. It offers a request/response model, resource discovery, and web concepts like URIs and media types, while keeping overhead low. It maps easily to HTTP and supports multicast.

plainLanguage.summary: CoAP is like the web, but made for tiny gadgets that cannot afford long messages. It lets small sensors and switches ask for and send information with very short notes.

questions: difference between confirmable and non-confirmable coap
subtitle: A compact, web-style request/response protocol that lets tiny devices on lossy networks talk to the Web.

tldr.problem: Very small devices, such as 8-bit microcontrollers on low-power, lossy networks, cannot afford HTTP and TCP, yet machine-to-machine applications like smart energy and building automation still want web-style access to resources.
tldr.mechanism: CoAP carries REST-style requests and responses in small binary messages over UDP, with a 4-byte header, optional retransmission for reliability, built-in resource discovery and multicast, and an easy mapping to HTTP.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7252 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 7959, RFC 8613, RFC 8974, RFC 9175 and RFC 9876, so read it together with those updates.

today: RFC 7252 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted, but it is updated by RFC 7959, RFC 8613, RFC 8974, RFC 9175 and RFC 9876. It remains the base specification of CoAP.

sections.title: Why a Web Protocol for Tiny Devices
sections.content:
The Web depends on the REST architecture, and the Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP) aims to bring it to the most constrained nodes (for example 8-bit microcontrollers with limited RAM and ROM) and networks such as 6LoWPAN. Those networks split IPv6 packets into small link-layer frames, and that fragmentation sharply lowers the chance that a packet is delivered. So one design goal is to keep messages small.

The RFC says plainly that the goal is not to blindly compress HTTP. CoAP realizes a subset of REST that is common with HTTP but optimized for machine-to-machine (M2M) use, and it adds things M2M needs: built-in discovery, multicast support and asynchronous message exchanges.

The main features are a UDP binding with optional reliability for unicast and multicast, low header overhead, URI and content-type support, simple proxy and caching, a stateless HTTP mapping and a security binding to Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS).
sections.plainLanguage: Big websites talk in long sentences. Tiny gadgets can only whisper a few words, so CoAP is a way to ask for things the way the web does, using very short notes.

sections.title: The CoAP Message
sections.content:
Every CoAP message sits in the data section of one UDP datagram. It starts with a fixed 4-byte header: a 2-bit Ver that MUST be 1, a 2-bit type T, a 4-bit Token Length TKL, an 8-bit Code and a 16-bit Message ID. After that come a Token of 0 to 8 bytes, zero or more options and an optional payload.

The type is one of four: Confirmable (0), Non-confirmable (1), Acknowledgement (2) or Reset (3). The Code is split into a 3-bit class and a 5-bit detail written c.dd; class 0 is a request, 2 is success, 4 is a client error and 5 is a server error. Code 0.00 is an Empty message that has only the 4-byte header.

Options are encoded as type-length-value entries in order of option number, using a delta from the previous option so that numbers stay small. If there is a payload, it is introduced by the one-byte Payload Marker 0xFF. A marker followed by a zero-length payload MUST be treated as a message format error.
sections.plainLanguage: A CoAP message is like a tiny envelope with a few boxes to tick at the top: what kind of note it is, what it asks, and a number so the reply can find its way back.

sections.title: Reliability Over UDP
sections.content:
Because UDP can lose, duplicate or reorder messages, CoAP adds a light reliability layer instead of copying TCP. A Confirmable message is retransmitted until the recipient sends an Acknowledgement (ACK) with the same Message ID, or a Reset (RST) if it lacks the context to process it. A Non-confirmable message is never acknowledged, which suits repeated sensor readings where eventual success is enough.

Retransmission uses stop-and-wait with exponential back-off. The first timeout is a random value between ACK_TIMEOUT (2 seconds) and ACK_TIMEOUT * ACK_RANDOM_FACTOR (1.5), and it doubles on each retry, up to MAX_RETRANSMIT (4) times. With the defaults, the whole span of transmissions is 45 seconds (MAX_TRANSMIT_SPAN) and the sender gives up after 93 seconds (MAX_TRANSMIT_WAIT).

Both message kinds carry a Message ID so that a recipient can detect duplicates. A Message ID must not be reused with the same endpoint within EXCHANGE_LIFETIME, which is 247 seconds by default. For congestion control, a client MUST NOT have more than NSTART (default 1) outstanding interactions with a given server, and a CoAP message SHOULD fit in a single IP packet; if the path MTU is unknown, 1280 bytes is assumed.
sections.plainLanguage: If you want to be sure your friend got a note, you ask them to wave back, and if they do not, you ask again after waiting longer each time. For unimportant notes, you just send them and do not wait for a wave.

sections.title: Requests, Responses and Methods
sections.content:
CoAP requests and responses are carried inside those messages. A request has a method (GET, POST, PUT or DELETE), a URI carried in options, and optionally a payload. GET is safe and idempotent; PUT and DELETE are idempotent; POST is neither, because what it does is decided by the origin server. A request with an unrecognized method MUST get a 4.05 (Method Not Allowed) response.

If the server can answer right away, it puts the response in the ACK. This is a piggybacked response. If it needs more time, it sends an Empty ACK first and the answer later in a new message, called a separate response; a response to a Non-confirmable request is always sent separately.

A client-chosen Token (0 to 8 bytes) matches a response to its request, independent of the Message ID. A client that is not using DTLS SHOULD use a randomized token to guard against spoofed responses, and one connected to the general Internet SHOULD use at least 32 bits of randomness.

Response codes echo HTTP in spirit: 2.01 Created, 2.02 Deleted, 2.03 Valid, 2.04 Changed, 2.05 Content, then 4.xx client errors such as 4.04 Not Found and 5.xx server errors such as 5.03 Service Unavailable. An unrecognized 4.xx or 5.xx code is treated like 4.00 or 5.00.
sections.plainLanguage: You hand over a note asking for something with a little ticket number on it. The answer either comes back right away stapled to the thank-you, or later in its own note carrying the same ticket number.

sections.title: Options, Content Formats and Caching
sections.content:
Metadata that HTTP would put in headers travels as CoAP options. The RFC defines Uri-Host, Uri-Port, Uri-Path, Uri-Query, Content-Format, Accept, Max-Age, ETag, Location-Path, Location-Query, Proxy-Uri, Proxy-Scheme, If-Match, If-None-Match and Size1. Each option is either critical or elective, and the RFC makes this depend on the option number itself: odd numbers are critical, even numbers are elective. An unrecognized elective option is silently ignored, while an unrecognized critical option in a Confirmable request gets a 4.02 (Bad Option) response.

The payload format is named by the Content-Format option, and the client can state its preference with Accept. If a response is an error and carries no Content-Format, its payload is a short human-readable diagnostic message in UTF-8.

Caching works from the response code rather than the request method. A response is fresh for the number of seconds in Max-Age, which defaults to 60, and a server that wants to prevent caching MUST send Max-Age of zero. A stale response can be revalidated with an ETag, and a 2.03 (Valid) answer means the stored copy can be reused.
sections.plainLanguage: Options are the little stickers on the note: what language it is written in, how long the answer stays good, and where the thing lives. Some stickers are so important that if you cannot read them you must not act on the note.

sections.title: Proxies and the HTTP Mapping
sections.content:
A proxy is a CoAP endpoint that makes requests on behalf of clients. Proxying is useful in constrained networks to limit traffic, to improve performance, to reach resources of sleeping devices, and for security reasons. A forward-proxy is chosen by the client, while a reverse-proxy stands in for origin servers and the client may not know it is there. A proxy treats options by whether they are Unsafe or Safe-to-Forward, a property also encoded in the option number.

Because CoAP follows REST, it is straightforward to map to HTTP. A cross-proxy converts methods, response codes, media types and options between CoAP and HTTP, in either direction, and the RFC gives per-method mappings for GET, PUT, DELETE and POST. No CONNECT-style function is defined for CoAP-to-CoAP proxies.
sections.plainLanguage: A proxy is a helper who runs errands for a tiny gadget, and some helpers can also translate between the gadget's short notes and the long letters the web uses.

sections.title: URIs, Discovery and Multicast
sections.content:
CoAP resources are named by URIs. The coap scheme uses UDP port 5683 by default, and the coaps scheme uses port 5684 and requires the datagrams to be secured with DTLS. The two are distinct namespaces and count as distinct origin servers even for the same host and port. A server offering resource discovery MUST support port 5683.

Resources are discovered with the CoRE Link Format from RFC 6690 under the /.well-known/ prefix, and the RFC adds a ct attribute that hints at a resource's content formats. Clients can also find servers with multicast to the "All CoAP Nodes" addresses: 224.0.1.187 for IPv4 and FF0X::FD for IPv6.

Multicast requests MUST be Non-confirmable, and a server that knows a request arrived by multicast MUST NOT answer with a Reset. Servers should not all answer at once. They pick a random moment within a leisure period, with a default of 5 seconds (DEFAULT_LEISURE), to avoid a flood of replies. Multicast cannot be carried over DTLS, so the security modes in this document do not apply to it.
sections.plainLanguage: Every thing a gadget offers has an address, like a street address. If you shout a question to a whole street, each neighbor waits a random moment before answering so they do not all talk at once.

sections.title: Securing CoAP and Its Risks
sections.content:
CoAP defines four security modes. NoSec has no protocol-level security, and RawPublicKey is the other mode that is mandatory to implement. PreSharedKey and Certificate complete the set. The last three use DTLS over UDP and the coaps scheme. After the handshake, DTLS adds about 13 bytes per datagram, not counting nonces, integrity values and padding. CoAP itself has no primitives for authentication or authorization; these come from DTLS, IPsec or object security.

The security considerations section warns of several threats. Complex parsers can have vulnerabilities. Responses can be larger than requests, so nodes that allow NoSec access can be used for amplification attacks, and servers SHOULD NOT give large amplification factors to unauthenticated requests. Spoofed source addresses are possible because UDP offers no way to verify them. Constrained nodes without a good source of entropy MUST NOT be used for processes that need it, such as key generation.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone can write a fake return address on a postcard, so CoAP can lock its notes with a secret code when it matters. It also tells helpers not to send back huge answers to strangers, so nobody can use them to flood someone else.

fields.name: TKL
fields.desc: Token length in bytes, 0 to 8; 9 to 15 are reserved.

fields.name: Code
fields.desc: 3-bit class and 5-bit detail, written c.dd; 0.00 is Empty.

fields.name: Message ID
fields.desc: Detects duplicates and matches ACK and RST to the message.
